title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 2: Bequeathing an Independent Court
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's January 11, 2009 Inquirer column on judicial independence as the indispensable first quality of a judge, opening with a sports-referee analogy (Pacquiao's win over De la Hoya means nothing without an impartial referee)

His 'four ins' of an ideal judge -- independence, integrity, intelligence, and industry -- with independence paramount: judges must be 'beholden to no one,' immune to the 'ships' (friendship, relationship, kinship, fellowship), and ready to 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall'

The Constitution's elaborate guarantees of judicial independence -- secure tenure to age 70, removal of justices only by impeachment, non-reducible salaries and an automatically released judiciary budget, a bar on laws lessening the Court's powers, and JBC-list appointments without legislative confirmation

His appeal to GMA, facing seven Supreme Court vacancies in 2009, to name a 'known independent' to the first one -- demolishing fears she would 'pack the Court to extend her reign beyond 2010' and instead 'bequeathing a great legacy: an independent and trustworthy Supreme Court'
sub_topics: The referee analogy: as in boxing or basketball, an 'impartial referee is non-negotiable' -- and impartiality matters even more 'in controversies involving the life, liberty, security, and well-being of our people'
The constitutional standard for magistrates: 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' which CJP restates as the four 'ins' (independence, integrity, intelligence, industry)

Independence first and foremost: judges must be 'beholden to no one,' decide only on legal merit, 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall,' and resist the 'ships' -- friendship, relationship, kinship, fellowship -- with the other three qualities reinforcing it

Constitutional guarantees of independence: tenure until age 70; Supreme Court justices removable only by impeachment, lower judges disciplined only by the Court (not the President or Congress); salaries not decreased during term; the judiciary's budget not cut below the prior year's and 'automatically and regularly released'

Structural insulation: Congress is barred from enacting laws that lessen the Court's powers and must secure the Court's 'advice and consent' to increase its appellate jurisdiction; the President appoints only from a JBC list of at least three, with no legislative confirmation

Guarding the JBC: civic groups like Bantay Korte Suprema (BKS) press for transparency; CJP's earlier worry that the Senate reorganization would 'decapitate' the BKS by replacing Pangilinan was eased by Escudero's prudence (open voting, Senate consensus), and he notes Puno (like CJP as CJ) votes only for the Court's own choices

The legacy appeal: with seven Supreme Court vacancies in 2009 (the JBC had sent a five-name list -- Villarama, Hormachuelos, Peralta, Villaruz, Villanueva), GMA should name a 'known independent' to the first to dispel fears of packing the Court, because once the people lose trust they 'turn to less than constitutional methods'

stances.claim: Independence is the first and indispensable judicial quality -- judges must be 'beholden to no one,' immune to the 'ships,' and willing to 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall' -- and the Constitution proves its preeminence by guaranteeing it at length (tenure, salary, budget, impeachment-only removal, JBC appointment) while barely mentioning the other qualities again.
stances.rhetorical_move: hierarchy-of-virtues argument: elevating independence above competence/integrity/industry and reading the Charter's emphasis as proof

stances.claim: GMA should name a 'known independent' to the first of the 2009 vacancies to 'demolish public apprehension that she would pack the Court to extend her reign beyond 2010' -- proving her critics wrong and 'bequeathing a great legacy: an independent and trustworthy Supreme Court.'
stances.rhetorical_move: legacy appeal: reframing a politically fraught appointment as a chance for the President to redeem her record

stances.claim: An independent Court is indispensable to democracy, because 'once our people lose trust in the Court, they will turn to less than constitutional methods to make their will prevail' -- a danger to the country and to GMA alike.
stances.rhetorical_move: stability argument: tying judicial independence to the prevention of extra-constitutional unrest

notable_anecdotes: The Pacquiao referee: CJP opens with Manny Pacquiao's win over Oscar de la Hoya, observing that 'had the referee been biased or unfair, Pacman's victory would have been skewed' -- his lead-in to the indispensability of an impartial judge.
The four 'ins': he recalls coining, across his books and speeches, the mnemonic of independence, integrity, intelligence and industry as the marks of an ideal judge.

Pangilinan-to-Escudero: he recounts his earlier fear that the Senate reorganization would 'decapitate' Bantay Korte Suprema by removing Pangilinan, eased when his replacement Escudero opted for open voting and a Senate consensus.
The five-name list: he names the JBC's nominees for the first 2009 vacancy and presses GMA to pick a 'known independent' to quiet fears of court-packing.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's January 11, 2009 Inquirer column, makes the case for judicial independence through a sports analogy: as Manny Pacquiao's win over Oscar de la Hoya would mean nothing under a biased referee, so 'an impartial referee is non-negotiable' -- and all the more in 'controversies involving the life, liberty, security, and well-being of our people.' The Constitution requires magistrates of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' which CJP restates as the four 'ins': independence, integrity, intelligence, and industry. Independence comes first -- judges must be 'beholden to no one,' decide only on legal merit, be immune to the 'ships' (friendship, relationship, kinship, fellowship), and 'let justice be done though the heavens may fall.' He shows the Charter's emphasis on independence through its many guarantees: tenure to age 70, removal of justices only by impeachment (lower judges disciplined only by the Court), salaries that cannot be decreased, a judiciary budget that cannot be cut below the prior year's and must be 'automatically and regularly released,' a bar on laws lessening the Court's powers, and appointments from a JBC list without legislative confirmation. He praises watchdogs like Bantay Korte Suprema and, easing an earlier worry, notes that Senator Escudero (replacing Pangilinan in the JBC) had shown prudence with open voting and a Senate consensus. Then comes his appeal: facing seven Supreme Court vacancies in 2009 (the JBC having sent a five-name list -- Villarama, Hormachuelos, Peralta, Villaruz, Villanueva), GMA should name a 'known independent' to the first to 'demolish public apprehension that she would pack the Court to extend her reign beyond 2010.' An independent Court is indispensable to democracy, he warns, for 'once our people lose trust in the Court, they will turn to less than constitutional methods' -- so now is the time for GMA to prove her critics wrong and start 'bequeathing a great legacy: an independent and trustworthy Supreme Court. Will she?'
